title: Physical Security
description: Physical security controls that protect people first, then facilities and equipment: control categories, layered defense, infrastructure, and fire detection and suppression.

nodes.title: Safety of people
nodes.description:
The one overarching, primary goal of physical security. People are the most valuable and important asset of any organization, so physical security controls must put the safety of people above everything else.
Physical security is also critical for confidentiality, integrity and availability:
- If you can touch the box, you own the box. An attacker with physical access to a device such as a firewall or server can easily take control of it, because equipment has built-in bypass controls such as factory reset buttons. So carefully control who can access facilities, specific rooms and equipment.
- UPSs and generators supply clean power, HVAC supplies air at the right temperature and humidity, and fire detection and suppression keep facilities from burning down.

children.title: Categories of Controls
children.description: The five categories of controls used in physical security: deter, delay, detect, assess and respond.

children.title: Deter, Delay, Detect, Assess, Respond
children.description:
- Deter: discourage trespassing, property damage, theft and intrusion, through signage and the environmental design of the building and the land around it.
- Delay: slow an attacker down, to buy time to detect and respond. Example: locks slow down an attacker trying to gain unauthorized access.
- Detect: notice that a risk has happened. Example: CCTV cameras.
- Assess: determine the method of attack and the target.
- Respond: take appropriate action to remediate the risk.

children.title: Layered Defense
children.description:
Never implement a control in isolation: if the only control protecting an asset fails, bad things happen.
Instead, place controls one behind another, from the outside of the site inward, so an attacker who gets past one still faces the next. At each level, combine preventive, detective and corrective controls, or in physical security terms, deterrent, detective, and assess and respond controls.

children.title: Perimeter
children.description:
Often the first layer of defense around a facility, such as an outside fence. The exterior walls of the building are another perimeter.
Best way to secure a perimeter: minimize the number of entrances and exits (doors).

children.title: Landscape
children.description:
The foliage around a building: trees and plants.
Maintain it so that cameras have clear sight lines, and so that an attacker cannot climb a tree and get into the building.

children.title: Grading
children.description:
How the land slopes around a building.
The ground should slope down and away from the building, so that in a flood the building stays dry, like an island, instead of sitting at the bottom of a lake.

children.title: Cameras
children.description:
Closed-circuit video systems are an important part of physical security. They act as a deterrent and a detective control, and can also be used for monitoring and auditing.
Cameras are primarily detective controls.

children.title: Passive Infrared Devices
children.description:
Motion sensors. Essentially very low-resolution cameras that detect infrared light: the heat emitted by objects in their field of view. When a warm-blooded person walks into the room, the infrared light increases and the movement is detected.
They must recalibrate automatically when the ambient air temperature changes.

children.title: Lighting
children.description:
A well-lit building helps deter crime.
Good lighting is also important for the safety of people.

children.title: Card Readers / Badges
children.description:
Card readers are electronic systems that control who is authorized to pass through a door into the building, or into rooms within it.
Two major types:
- Contact: the employee swipes the card through the reader (older magnetic readers).
- Contactless: the employee only holds the card near the reader (RFID, Radio Frequency ID).
Badges are simply a card with the employee's name and photo.

children.title: Doors / Mantraps
children.description:
Doors are the primary way to control who can enter the building and specific parts of it.
Tailgating or piggybacking is a very common and successful social engineering attack on them: an intruder follows an authorized person through after they unlock it. Prevent it with specialized entrances: mantraps or turnstiles.
The specialized entrance is two doors, one after the other, around a small space. Unlock the first, step inside, close it behind you, and only then can you unlock the second.

children.title: Locks
children.description:
A perfect example of a delay control. Given time, an attacker will pick, force or break a lock and get in.
Because locks only delay, never use them in isolation. Remember layered defense (defense in depth).
For combination locks, one of the most important security factors is the complexity of the combination.

children.title: Mechanical
children.description: Locks operated by physical means, such as a key or a dial. Examples: keyed locks, mechanical combination locks and magnetic locks.

children.title: Digital
children.description: Electronic locks. Examples: proximity or RFID locks, electronic combination locks and biometric locks.

children.title: Windows
children.description:
Windows let in natural light, but they are often the weak link in a building's perimeter.
The glass comes in many types, such as plate, tempered, laminated, wired and polycarbonate. You do not need to memorize them.
Instead, understand the sensors that detect when the glass has been broken.

children.title: Shock
children.description: Sensors attached directly to a pane of glass. They detect the small vibration created when the pane breaks.

children.title: Glass break
children.description: Acoustic sensors that listen for the distinctive sound of a pane shattering. They do not need to be attached to the glass.

children.title: Walls
children.description: Critical to physical security: it is hard to secure a building without exterior and interior walls.

children.title: Skimming
children.description: Criminals use an electronic device to steal card information from a valid transaction. Examples: a device on a bank machine that records your debit card number, a device on a point-of-sale machine that copies your credit card details, or an attacker near a secure door who wirelessly records the RFID communication from your employee card.

children.title: Infrastructure
children.description: The three major infrastructure services critical to the operation of a facility: network, power and HVAC.

children.title: Network
children.description: A reliable connection to the internet, the largest distributed network in the world, and/or to the organization's other locations.

children.title: Power
children.description:
Almost all equipment needs electricity, and few businesses could keep working without electronic systems. So security is very concerned with a consistent supply of clean power.
Clean power does not mean renewable here. It means AC (Alternating Current) power that oscillates at a steady 60 Hz (50 Hz in many countries), with no noise or distortion on the line: a perfect sine wave.
UPSs and generators are the important devices for a consistent supply of clean power.

children.title: UPS
children.description:
Essentially a giant battery that provides instant but short-term power, until the generator has time to start up and come online.
Full name: Uninterruptible Power Supply.

children.title: Generator
children.description:
Typically a large diesel engine connected to an alternator.
Provides long-term backup power: hours or even days, depending on how much fuel is on site.

children.title: Power Outages
children.description:
A complete loss of power:
- Blackout: no power for a long period.
- Fault: a momentary loss of power.

children.title: Power Degradation
children.description:
Too little or too much power:
- Brownout: an intentional reduction of voltage by the utility company.
- Sag / dip: a short period of low voltage.
- Surge: a period of too much voltage. A momentary one is a spike. Think lightning strike.

children.title: HVAC
children.description:
The systems that supply air to a building at the correct temperature and humidity, and filter it.
Full name: Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning.

children.title: Temperature
children.description:
The main reason to bring cool air into a data center is to cool the equipment and keep it operating within the desired temperature range.
Ideal range, defined by ASHRAE (the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers): 18 °C to 27 °C (64.4 °F to 80.6 °F). Most office buildings and data centers are built to these ranges.
Exam questions list both Celsius and Fahrenheit.

children.title: Humidity
children.description:
HVAC also supplies air at the right humidity. Too dry gives static electricity; too humid gives condensation. Both are bad.
Ideal relative humidity (ASHRAE): 40% to 60%.

children.title: Air Quality
children.description:
HVAC filters the air to remove dust and other contaminants. In a data center, air is sucked into and through servers and other equipment. Contaminants could clog the equipment and cause shorts, or make it overheat and fail.
Know the term positive pressurization: clean, filtered air is blown into the data center at slightly above ambient pressure. If there are cracks in the walls, or someone opens a door, clean air is forced out, so dirty air and contaminants cannot get in.

children.title: Fire Detection
children.description:
Fire is a significant risk. As with any risk, control it with a combination of preventive, detective and corrective controls:
- Prevent: limit or eliminate combustible materials. You can never prevent fire entirely.
- Detect: detect a fire as quickly as possible.
- Correct: suppress the fire as quickly as possible.
Three major types of fire detection: flame, smoke and heat detectors.
Which detects a fire earliest? There is always smoke before a fire, and the main concern is flaming (fast) fires, so pick ionization detectors.

children.title: Flame (Infrared)
children.description:
Flame detectors detect the infrared and ultraviolet light that flames create.
They are essentially video cameras pointed at something you are worried might catch fire.

children.title: Smoke
children.description:
There is always smoke before a fire, so smoke detectors are one of the best ways to detect a fire as early as possible.
Two major types: ionization and photo-electric.

children.title: Ionization
children.description: Respond more quickly to flaming, or fast, fires.

children.title: Photo-electric
children.description: Detect smoke when it blocks or scatters a beam of light inside the detector. Respond more quickly to smoldering fires.

children.title: Dual
children.description:
Combine ionization and photo-electric detection in one device.
Most good-quality detectors today are dual detectors.

children.title: Heat (Thermal)
children.description:
Heat detectors, also called thermal or rate-of-rise detectors, are temperature sensors that watch for a rapid rise in temperature.
If the temperature spikes rapidly, you probably have a fire.

children.title: Fire Suppression
children.description:
Two major types of fire suppression system: water-based and gas-based.
Water-based systems are cheaper, but water and expensive electrical equipment in a data center are a terrible combination. So gas-based systems are cost-justified in data centers.

children.title: Water
children.description:
Common in office buildings, hotels and other spaces where some water will not destroy millions of dollars' worth of equipment.
Know four types of water-based system.

children.title: Wet, Dry, Pre-action, Deluge
children.description:
- Wet (wet pipe): the pipes always hold pressurized water, waiting to be released. The cheapest, but with big downsides: it cannot be used where pipes might freeze, and with pressurized water in the pipes at all times, leaks are inevitable.
- Dry (dry pipe): looks the same as wet pipe, but the pipes are dry, filled with pressurized gas. Water floods into the pipes only when needed.
- Pre-action: the pipes stay dry until a fire detection system triggers and fills them with water. Each sprinkler head then opens only when heat activates it. The two steps reduce accidental water release.
- Deluge: the pipes are dry and the sprinkler heads are open. When triggered, a large volume of water flows out of all heads at once.

children.title: Gas
children.description:
Systems that flood a room with a suppression agent instead of water.
Some displace the oxygen in a room: no oxygen, no fire. But no oxygen also means no human life, so safety systems must let people leave the data center before the agent is released.
Others interrupt the chemical, exothermic process that is fire.

children.title: INERGEN, Argonite, FM-200, Aero-K
children.description:
The four major gas-based fire suppression agents to know:
- INERGEN
- Argonite
- FM-200
- Aero-K
Halon is deliberately not listed. It was traditionally used in data centers, but its production has been banned globally because it destroys the ozone layer. Do not pick Halon on the exam.

children.title: Extinguisher
children.description:
Fire extinguishers: the red devices hanging on walls everywhere.
Five classes, each for a different type of fire and using different suppression agents:
- A (Ash): common combustibles. Water, foam, dry chemicals.
- B (Boil): liquids. Gas, CO₂, foam, dry chemicals.
- C (Current): electrical. Gas, CO₂, dry chemicals.
- D (Dense): combustible metals. Dry powders.
- K (Kitchen): commercial kitchens. Wet chemicals.
The one class to highlight is C: for electrical fires, the type you might have in a data center. Class C extinguishers often use CO₂ (carbon dioxide) as the suppression agent.

children.title: CO₂
children.description:
An excellent fire suppression agent for data centers: it is non-corrosive (it will not damage expensive equipment), leaves no residue and does not conduct electricity.
It works by displacing oxygen, so at the levels needed to flood a room it can suffocate people. Everyone must leave before it is released.
